content_blocks.text:
Paste text into a consumer AI tool and that text leaves your building. It travels to a model running on someone else's servers. Depending on the tool and its settings, it might be retained, logged, reviewed by a person checking quality, or used to train the next version of the model. Some tools promise none of that. Others do all of it by default and let you opt out. Most people never check which kind they are using.

This failure sits entirely on your side of the screen: sensitive information going into a tool that has no business holding it. The mechanics take a sentence to explain. Deciding what is safe to paste is the part that takes attention. If you manage people, the norm you set here is the one your team will copy, and if you manage no one, the same call still lands on you every time you open a chat window with real work in front of you.
What happens to what you type

The question worth asking is a concrete one. Where does your input go, who can see it, and what are they allowed to do with it? A tool your organisation has vetted and licensed answers those questions in your favour. A free account someone signed up for on their own does not.
What counts as sensitive
Most people picture passwords and credit card numbers. At a management level the real exposure is broader and a good deal more mundane.

cards.body: Names, contact details, salaries, performance notes, health or HR matters. Anything that identifies a person carries legal obligations, however harmless it feels in the moment.
cards.title: Personal data

cards.body: Unreleased financials, pricing strategy, deal terms, roadmaps, merger and acquisition discussions. The budget you assemble before a decision meeting is exactly this.
cards.title: Commercial secrets

cards.body: Anything shared with you under an agreement: partner data, customer records, supplier terms. It is not yours to expose, and the obligation is often written into a contract.
cards.title: Third-party confidential

cards.body: Board material, legal advice, security details, anything covered by confidentiality. Fluent output is worthless if the input should never have left the room.
cards.title: Internal and privileged

content_blocks.text: A useful test before you paste: if this text turned up in a competitor's inbox or on a news site, would it cause a problem? If the answer is yes, it does not go into an unapproved tool.
Approved tools, in practice

"Approved" means your organisation has done the diligence: checked where the data goes, signed terms that forbid training on your input, and confirmed the tool meets the standards your sector requires. It can look identical to the free version. The difference lives in the contract and the configuration, well out of sight of the interface.
The same brand name can be safe or unsafe depending on the account. A licensed enterprise tenant and a personal free login are different tools wearing the same logo.

The practical move is narrow: know which tools your organisation has sanctioned for which kinds of data, and make that answer easy for your team to find. When the answer is ambiguous, people improvise rather than pause.
Shadow AI is the real risk

Shadow AI is the use of unapproved tools for real work: the marketing manager drafting on a personal account, the analyst pasting next quarter's budget into whatever tool ranked first in a search. It rarely comes from bad intent. Usually a good tool was just easier to reach than the sanctioned one.

This is where leadership matters more than IT. If the approved path is slow, hidden, or worse than the free alternative, people route around it, and you cannot police your way out of that. You close the gap by making the sanctioned tool the path of least resistance, and by being clear out loud about what belongs where.
Concrete behaviours

Strip the specifics before you paste. You can often get the same quality of help by removing names, figures, and identifiers while keeping the structure, so ask the model to pressure-test the shape of a budget case with the real numbers pulled out rather than left in. Use the approved tool for anything real, and default to it even when it is marginally less convenient. When you are unsure whether something is sensitive, treat it as if it is. And set the expectation with your team plainly, because they will match what you actually do, not what the policy says.

questions.explanation: Budget and pricing figures are a commercial secret. Keep AI in play by using a vetted tool or by removing the sensitive specifics before you paste. Turning history off does not change where an unapproved tool sends your input or what its terms permit.

content_blocks.text: You have hired someone who starts in two weeks, and you want a real onboarding plan: week one, who they meet, what good looks like by month one. A model gives you a usable first pass in about a minute. Whether you bin that pass or send it comes down to a handful of deliberate moves in the prompt.

By now you can write a clear prompt and run the review-and-refine loop. This lesson is the toolkit you reach for inside that loop: the specific levers that lift output from acceptable to good. Each takes seconds, and you will use each dozens of times a week. The onboarding plan is a good place to watch them work one at a time.

If you don't manage anyone, the same moves apply to any structured document you own: a runbook, a wiki page, the checklist you run through yourself whenever a new project spins up.
Show an example, do not just describe one

The fastest way to tell a model what you want is to show it. A style described in adjectives, "concise, warm, practical", leaves the model guessing at what those words mean to you. One concrete example takes the guessing away.

Write a single onboarding item the way you want the rest to read: owner, task, and the week it falls in, in that order. Paste one line at the register you are after. Hand over the header row of the table you already have in your head. The model matches a pattern it can see far more reliably than one you describe, and one task written your way sets the shape for the twenty that follow.
One good example is worth ten adjectives. When you catch yourself piling up describing words, stop and paste a sample instead.
Assign a role to shift the lens

Telling the model who to be changes what it pays attention to. Ask it to review your onboarding plan and you get a flat, generic once-over. Ask it to review the plan as a brand-new joiner reading it on day one, someone who knows none of your systems or shorthand, and it starts flagging the jargon, the login nobody requested, and the week-one task that quietly assumes a fortnight of context.

A role sets a lens for a particular kind of scrutiny or a particular reader: a finance reviewer hunting for soft numbers, a sceptical peer poking holes in a timeline, a non-technical reader tripping over jargon. For an onboarding plan, the most useful reviewer is often the new hire themselves, the one person who will hit every gap you left in. Point that lens at the draft before it reaches them, and you find the holes while they are still cheap to close.
Specify the format, not just the content

You can dictate the exact shape of the output: how many sections, what each one covers, a length ceiling, the columns of a table. You met format as one of the baseline levers already. What matters here is that a tight format spec compounds with the others and cuts a whole round off the refine loop.

Take the plan again. "Build me an onboarding plan" hands you prose you then have to carve into a schedule. "Organise the first month into four weekly blocks, each a table with columns for task, owner, and what done looks like, plus one line on the goal for that week" hands you something already shaped like a document you can send. The specified version asks no more of the model, only more intention from you about the shape.

There is a negative half you already know: naming what to leave out. It carries over. A format spec is as much about what you exclude, no filler, no motivational preamble, as what you put in, and it stacks cleanly with a role or a self-critique instruction.
Make the model critique itself

Here is the lever most people never touch. Once the model has produced the plan, tell it to turn on its own work: "List the three weakest points in this onboarding plan." "Where would a new joiner get stuck in week one?" "What did I leave out that a real first week needs?"

With nothing to defend, the model will often name genuine gaps: the access request nobody kicked off, the introduction you skipped, the first task that assumes context the new person has not been handed yet. You stay the judge of which flags are fair. But a self-critique pass surfaces candidates for revision faster than reading the draft cold, and it costs you a single line. It pays off most on anything a person will actually live by, like the plan a new hire follows through week one.
A self-critique pass finds weak spots; it does not fix them. It will list problems and then, if you let it, paper over them with confident filler. You decide which gaps matter and how to close them.
Combining levers

The levers stack. A strong onboarding prompt might set a role, fix the format, and end with a self-critique all at once: "As an experienced manager onboarding a new team member, draft a four-week plan as weekly tables, then list the two things a first-timer would still find confusing." You won't need all four every time. For anything you will send onward, or that a new hire will lean on, layering two or three of them is the cheapest quality gain you have.

content_blocks.text: The prompt you type is only half the instruction the model follows. The other half was written before you arrived, and it explains most of the behaviour that catches you off guard.

Every response a model produces is shaped by two layers of instruction: the prompt you send, and a standing set of instructions you never see. Knowing both exist changes how you read what comes back, and how much of a tool's behaviour you can actually change.
The prompt: what you send

A prompt is any input you give the model: a question, an instruction, a document to summarise, a set of notes to turn into a task list. The model takes your prompt, adds whatever else is already sitting in the context window, and builds a response out of all of it.

The term gets used loosely. Sometimes it means a single message; sometimes it means the whole approach to phrasing a request well. Either way the principle holds: what you put in shapes what you get back. Ask a support tool to "reply to this complaint" and you get something generic and cautious. Tell it the customer has been waiting nine days, that you want an apology without admitting fault, and that a goodwill credit should be offered in the last line, and you get a reply you can almost send as it stands.

You don't need the full craft yet; that comes in the next module. One instinct is enough for now: the model fills gaps with assumptions, and its assumptions are not always yours. A vague prompt fails quietly. It hands you a confident, plausible answer to a question you didn't quite ask, and nothing in the output flags the gap.
The system prompt: what was set before you arrived

Before your first message, the model has already been handed a set of standing instructions. This is the system prompt. It runs behind the interface, never shows up in the chat thread, and shapes how the model behaves across the whole conversation: what role to play, what tone to strike, what to focus on, what to refuse.

Every AI tool you open already has one. Take the customer support assistant behind a company's help chat. Its system prompt is what turns a general model into that assistant, fixing the tone, the policies it can quote, the refunds it is allowed to mention, and the topics it must hand to a human. When you set a persona or global instructions in a tool that offers them, you are writing a lightweight system prompt of your own.
Builders use a system prompt to configure a model once, for everyone who touches the tool. You use prompts to steer it in the moment, for the task in front of you.
Why the difference matters to you

You may never write a system prompt. Knowing one is always running still changes how you read what you see.

When a model refuses a reasonable request, softens an answer, or keeps forcing a format you didn't ask for, reach for the system prompt before you blame your own wording. A standing rule you cannot see is often the thing steering the model, and once you spot that, you either work around it or move to a tool configured for what you actually need.

It also sets your expectations about control. The system prompt sets the stage; your prompt directs the scene inside it. You have real influence over the second layer and none over the first, which is why the tool you pick matters as much as the wording of any single request.

cards.body: Written by you, during the conversation, and visible in the chat. It directs the task in front of you right now. This is the layer you control.
cards.title: Prompt

cards.body: Written by the builder or admin before the conversation, and never shown to you. It shapes the role, tone, and limits the model follows across the whole session. You inherit it rather than set it.
cards.title: System prompt

content_blocks.text: What this buys you

Two takeaways carry into the rest of the track. Output quality tracks input quality: the sharper and more specific your prompt, the more usable the result, and that skill is entirely yours to build. And when a tool behaves in a way your prompt never asked for, look past your own wording to the instructions you cannot see. Both come down to the same recognition. You are always working inside a frame someone else set, and you steer with the one layer that belongs to you.

questions.explanation: Restrictive behaviour that holds across a whole conversation usually traces to the system prompt: standing instructions set by the builder that you cannot see. Recognising this points you to work around it or switch tools rather than blame your own wording.

content_blocks.text: If you send it, it's yours. The credit when it lands, and the fallout when it doesn't.

You feed the model your rough notes from a performance review and it hands back a clean, confident write-up in seconds. That fluency is why accountability is where this module ends: the easier the output is to accept, the easier it is to pass on something you never actually checked. The tool does not sign the review. You do.
Delegation moves the work, not the responsibility

You can hand the write-up to a model the way you would hand it to someone on your team. What you cannot hand over is ownership of the result. When that review lands in the record, or goes up to an HR partner who trusts your read, the model's part in it is invisible, and your decision to send it is not. If you manage no one, the same thing holds for the customer reply or the wiki entry you draft with AI and put out as your own work: you are still the one who chose to release it.

None of this is new. You were always answerable for work done in your name by other people. AI just makes the review step easier to skip, because the draft arrives polished and instant. A thin draft from a colleague looks thin. A hallucinated figure inside a fluent summary looks fine right up until someone acts on it.

A confident tone on the page tells you nothing about whether the facts behind it hold. Output earns exactly as much trust as the checking you have put into it, and it goes out as your work, not the tool's.
Where the accountability bites

The consequences land in specific places. A performance summary that overstates a target someone actually hit can sink a promotion case. The model can also attribute a quote to a colleague who never said it, and that line then sits in a record people will read for years. A single reworded policy sentence can change what the policy permits, with the exposure surfacing only once someone relies on it.

In each case the model did nothing unusual. It predicted plausible text, which is all it ever does. The failure was that a person forwarded that text without owning it.
Attribution and intellectual property
Attribution is yours to sort out before you rely on the output. Look at what went into the draft, and at what comes out of it.

cards.body: A model can reproduce text close to what it was trained on, and it will echo whatever you fed it, including material you had no right to reuse. Paste in a competitor document or a copyrighted source, pass the result along, and the provenance problem is now yours.
cards.title: What went in

cards.body: AI output generally cannot be claimed as original authored work the way human writing can, and the rules vary by jurisdiction and context. When originality or attribution carries weight, such as external publication or anything legal or contractual, treat provenance as something you must be able to account for.
cards.title: What comes out

content_blocks.text: For most internal work the bar is simple: you should be able to say where a claim came from and stand behind it. If you cannot, it is not ready to leave your hands.
What owning it looks like in practice

Owning the output is what lets you use AI with confidence rather than caution. When you verify, check provenance, and stand behind the result, you can move fast, because you are not gambling on something you never read.

Set the tone for the people around you. If leaders forward unchecked AI output, the lesson everyone absorbs is that fluent equals finished. If they visibly own what they send, checking the figures and questioning the sources, that becomes the standard others copy.

content_blocks.text: You do not need to write Markdown to work well with AI. Recognising it is enough: knowing why your AI tool keeps producing it, and how to get clean text back when a destination will not display it properly.

Markdown is a lightweight way to add structure to plain text using ordinary characters: a hash for a heading, asterisks for bold, a hyphen for a bullet. That is all it is. It's punctuation for structure rather than a coding skill, and it takes about two minutes to learn to read.

It matters because it turns up everywhere AI touches. When your tool hands back an answer with headings, bold key terms, and neat bullets, it's writing Markdown. Documentation, notes apps, and plenty of editors use the same conventions. Knowing what you're looking at makes you faster and spares you a few avoidable annoyances.
Why the model outputs it

Structure is easier to produce and easier to read than a wall of prose, so models default to it. The same logic runs the other way. A prompt you organise with a heading and a few bullets is easier for the model to follow than one long paragraph. Say you're turning a sprint's worth of changes into release notes: give it the fixes, the new features, and the breaking changes as three separate points, and it tracks each one instead of losing them mid-sentence. You already do this when you write a good prompt, and Markdown is just the tidy way to lay it out.
The handful of patterns worth recognising
You will never need most of the syntax. These few cover almost everything you will meet.

cards.body: A hash then a space makes a heading; two hashes make a smaller sub-heading. Text wrapped in double asterisks is bold; single asterisks is italic.
cards.title: Headings and emphasis

cards.body: A hyphen and a space starts a bullet. A number, a dot, and a space starts a numbered list. This is what turns a set of points into a scannable list.
cards.title: Lists

cards.body: A greater-than sign and a space marks a quoted block. Text wrapped in backticks shows as monospace, used for things like file names or a single command.
cards.title: Quotes and code

content_blocks.text: The one thing that trips people up

Markdown only becomes clean formatting when something renders it. A chat window renders it, so you see tidy headings and bullets. A plain email field or a basic text box usually does not, so you get the raw symbols instead.

So when you paste those release notes into an email and they arrive cluttered with hashes, double asterisks, and stray hyphens, nothing has gone wrong. You are looking at unrendered Markdown. Paste it somewhere that renders it, since most modern document and mail editors do, or ask the tool for plain text with no formatting. For notes going out to the whole team or to a customer, that quick check is worth making before you hit send.

Before forwarding AI output, look at how it renders where it is going. Symbols where formatting should be mean you are sending raw Markdown. Ask for plain text, or paste it into an editor that renders it.

content_blocks.text: Say you ask an AI to update the risk register for a project you run. One version drafts from the notes you paste in. Another opens the tracker itself, reads the past fortnight, spots a supplier delay slipping from amber to red, and flags two mitigations already overdue. Same request, very different reach.

So far you have met AI as something you talk to. You send a prompt, get text back, take it from there. That is the base case, and it is where most people stay. Two developments push past it. One is AI that takes actions instead of only answering. The other is AI that plugs into the tools and data where your work already lives. You will not build either yourself, but anyone deciding where AI fits needs to recognise what they are and where the risk moves.
Chat is the doorway, not the whole house. The versions of AI that change how work actually gets done can act on your behalf and reach into the systems where that work sits.
From answering to acting: agents

A standard chat model responds one message at a time, and you stay in the loop for every step. It drafts, you read, you decide what comes next. An agent works differently. You hand it a goal, and it takes several steps toward that goal on its own: running a search, reading a file, drafting a result, checking what it produced, moving on to the next step. Your input along the way is far lighter.

Back to the risk register. Ask a chat model and it structures whatever you handed it. An agent could go and find the material first, pull the recent status updates, cross-reference them against last quarter's entries, and hand back a marked-up draft. Several steps, little supervision.

That autonomy is where the value sits, and where the risk sits with it. More unsupervised steps mean more places a wrong turn goes unseen. A single confident-but-wrong answer is easy to catch when you read every reply. A wrong step buried three actions deep in an agent run is not: the overdue mitigation it quietly dropped, or the risk it rated low because it never saw the email that would have raised the flag.
The more steps an AI takes without you, the more the job shifts from checking the reply to verifying the outcome. Autonomy raises the value and the stakes at the same time.
Reaching your systems: connectors and MCP

An agent that cannot touch anything is only a talker. What lets AI reach past the chat window is a connector: a pre-built link between an AI tool and an outside system, whether that is your files, an email thread, a document store, or the tracker holding your risk register. Point the tool at that tracker and it can read what is there. The link that makes it possible is the connector.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard that keeps those links consistent. Rather than every AI tool needing a custom build for every system, MCP gives them a shared format to speak, so a connector built once works across tools. Think of a universal plug instead of a drawer full of mismatched adapters.

Here is the short version for you. Connectors turn AI from a clever writing partner into something wired into where your work already sits. That is what makes it useful, and it is also why access, permissions, and oversight are worth asking about before you switch it on.

content_blocks.text: What to take from this

You are not being asked to set any of this up. The how lives in the tool-specific tracks. What matters now is recognition. When someone says an AI can just handle a multi-step job, hear agent, and ask how the outcome gets checked. When a tool offers to connect to your inbox, your files, or that project tracker, hear connector, and ask who approved the access and what it can see.

content_blocks.text:
A model does not look up answers. It predicts text, one token at a time, always reaching for the most plausible next chunk. That single habit explains two surprises at once: why the same prompt can give you two different answers, and why it can hand you a confident, well-formed fact that is simply untrue.

Last lesson was about what goes into a model. This one is about what comes out, and why it is both less fixed and less reliable than the fluent writing makes it look.
Prediction, not retrieval

A search engine finds text that already exists and returns it. A model works differently. It builds each answer from scratch, choosing every word because it plausibly follows what came before. Nothing is retrieved. The model produces text that resembles what it learned from, without ever checking a verified record of what is true.

That resemblance is usually good enough to be useful. But the model optimises for plausibility, not truth, and almost everything that surprises you about AI, the inconsistency and the confident mistakes, comes back to that one fact.
Why the same prompt varies

Ask the same question twice and you can get two different answers. That is by design, not a fault.

At each step the model does not lock onto one guaranteed next word. It weighs many candidates, each with its own probability, and picks from among them. A setting called **temperature** controls how much freedom it has in that choice. Turn it low and the model stays close to the single most likely path: steady and repeatable, the right setting for pulling figures out of a report or forcing messy notes into a fixed structure. Turn it up and the model ranges into less likely paths, which reads as more varied and more creative.

Temperature is not a quality dial. A higher setting produces more variation and more drift; it does not produce a better answer. Most tools run at a moderate default you never see, which is why the same prompt rarely comes back the same way twice.

So whether that variability helps or hurts comes down entirely to what you asked for. When you need one exact result every time, it is a liability. When you want options, it is an asset: ask for three ways to open a difficult message to your team, or a few different angles on a recommendation you are about to send up, and the spread is the point. Same mechanism, opposite value.
Why it can be confidently wrong

The same mechanism produces the failure that catches people off guard: a **hallucination**, where the model states something plausible-sounding that is simply false.

This is the mechanism working exactly as designed. Ask for a citation, a figure, or a name the model was not well trained on, and it does the only thing it can: it produces the text that most plausibly fits. A convincing reference to a paper that was never published. A precise-looking number with nothing behind it. It all arrives in the same fluent, authoritative tone as everything else, because producing authoritative-sounding text is the one thing the model is built to do.

The confidence in the writing tells you nothing about whether the content is right. The model gives no signal of its own uncertainty. A fabricated figure and a correct one reach you in the same even voice.
Fluency is not evidence. A model that sounds certain is not the same as a model that is right, and it produces that certain tone whether or not the facts behind it hold up.

Hallucinations cluster exactly where the mechanism predicts: on specific facts the model has little exposure to, like names, dates, figures, technical specs, and references to real documents. They are far rarer when the model works from material you supplied, such as rewriting a clause in plain language, restructuring notes, or reasoning over a document you pasted in. Take a competitor brief you are building from your own scattered notes. Pulling those notes into a clean structure is low-risk. The moment the model volunteers a market-share figure you never gave it, the risk climbs.
Two behaviours, one cause

Understanding that is not the same as knowing what to do about it; checking output and judging where the real risk sits come later in the track. For now, form one instinct: the more a task turns on specific facts, figures, or names, the less the model's confidence is worth.

content_blocks.text: This path is here to make you effective with AI at work, fast and without the guesswork. By the end you will know what to hand off, what to check, and what to keep for yourself.

Most people meet AI through trial and error. A few results that genuinely impress, a few that quietly embarrass, and no reliable sense of when to trust the thing. That is a slow and expensive way to learn. This path swaps that guesswork for judgment, so you can direct AI on purpose and help set the tone for how the people around you use it.
What this path is

A structured route from "I have heard AI is useful" to "I know where it pays off and where it does not." It is built for people who lead work and make decisions, and it stays just as useful if you manage no one and simply want to do your own job well with AI in it.

It is not a tour of buttons and menus, and that is on purpose. Tools get renamed and rebuilt every few months; the judgment about when to trust them lasts a lot longer. So the focus stays on what holds steady: what these systems are good at, how they fail, how to steer them, and where the responsibility stays with you.
What you will be able to do
By the end, none of the choices that actually matter will be a guess.

content_blocks.text: How it is structured

Short lessons, grouped into modules, in a deliberate order. The early modules build a working picture of what AI is and how it behaves. The middle ones teach you to steer it and to catch it when it goes wrong. The last modules turn all of that into a way of working: deciding what to delegate, building your own instincts, and putting the whole kit to work on a task you do again and again.

Each lesson adds one idea and assumes the ones before it. That order is doing real work, so resist the urge to jump ahead. A point from module five lands far better once modules two and three have given you something to hang it on.
Lessons build on each other. Skipping ahead is the fastest way to end up confused about something a two-minute earlier lesson would have made obvious.
How to use it

Read actively rather than passively. The lessons only pay off when they change how you handle a real task afterwards. Keep something concrete in mind as you go: a customer complaint you want to answer well, a budget review before a decision meeting, the release notes nobody has had time to write yet. Those are the kinds of jobs the later lessons work through, and every idea sticks better once you have tested it against work you actually own.

Short lessons, a little practice in between, and some honesty with yourself about what worked will take you further than reading straight through in one sitting.

content_blocks.text: When someone asks "can AI do this?", the honest answer is another question: which model, and how capable is it?

In most workplace conversations, "AI" is shorthand for a large language model, an LLM, running behind a chat window. Knowing what that actually is, and how one model differs from the next, changes how you brief it, what you trust it with, and where your budget goes.
What a large language model is

An LLM is trained on huge amounts of text to do one thing: predict what text should plausibly come next, given what came before. That sounds narrow, but in practice it covers a lot of ground. The same trained system can draft a stakeholder update, pull a batch of open-ended survey comments into a themed summary, rewrite a dense clause in plain language, or turn scribbled notes into a clean action list.

The reach is real, and so are the limits. The model has no memory of your last conversation unless the tool feeds it back in. It does not see live information unless something connects it to a source that does. And because it produces plausible text rather than looking things up, it is usually right and occasionally, confidently, wrong.
Model versus tool

A model is the specific trained system that does the predicting. It has a name and a version. The tool is the product you open to reach it: the chat window, the app in your browser. When you type into that window, the tool hands your prompt to a model and passes the answer back. Keep the tool the same, swap the model behind it, and the result changes.

That matters because providers do not ship a single model. They ship a family, each member tuned to a different balance of speed, cost, and reasoning power.
Capability tiers

Within a family, models come in tiers. Each tier trades speed and cost against raw capability, and most providers follow the same shape: a fast, cheap model for high-volume routine work, a balanced model for everyday tasks, and a top model built for hard reasoning.

cards.body: Quick and low cost, made for simple high-volume work: short summaries, quick rewrites, routine drafting. Capable enough for most everyday asks.

content_blocks.text: The Claude family is a clear example. Haiku is the fast, economical tier, Sonnet the balanced one, and Opus the most capable. Other providers sell the same range under their own names. A model name points to a specific version, and newer versions are usually better across the board. The fast tier is a different point on the curve, not a cheaper knock-off of the good one.
Why the choice matters

Picking a model is a design decision. Say you have a few hundred free-text responses from a customer survey to summarise before a review meeting. If you just want the recurring themes grouped and counted, the fast tier does it well, and running the top model over the same batch buys you nothing but a longer wait and a bigger bill. But if you need it to weigh contradictory feedback, catch the quiet complaint that signals a real problem, and tell you which themes actually matter, that is reasoning work, and the fast tier will hand you a smooth summary that misses the point. Reach for the top tier on the hard read. Keep the fast tier for the routine roll-up.

Turn every vague "can AI do this?" into something you can act on: which tool, which model, how capable, and where does it fall short? That question is what separates deliberate use from hoping for the best.

content_blocks.text: You hand AI the all-hands script, skim the first paragraph, and it sounds like you on a good day. The reflex is to forward it and get on with something else. That reflex is what this lesson is about.

Before you decide where AI fits in your work, start by disarming two reflexes. The first is the hype: the feeling that AI is a step from replacing whole functions, so the only sane move is to hand it everything. The second is the dismissal: the feeling that it is a party trick that makes things up and cannot be trusted with anything that counts. Both fail in the same place. Each one treats AI as a single verdict rather than a tool with a shape.
Why the extremes both mislead

The hype misleads because fluent output is not the same as sound output. AI writes text that reads as confident and finished whether or not it is correct. That polish is persuasive, and persuasive-but-wrong costs you more than obviously-wrong, because it is the version that slips through unread and surfaces later.

The dismissal misleads because the same tool, pointed at the right work, is genuinely fast and good. Someone who tried it once, got a bad answer, and wrote the whole thing off has judged it on a single sample. That is the standard they would never accept from a colleague.
The most expensive stance is certainty in either direction. Being sure AI is infallible and being sure it is useless both stop you from finding where the line actually sits.
The stance that pays

What works instead is calibration. You walk in expecting AI to be strong at some things and weak at others, and you read every output as a draft you are accountable for rather than a result you can forward unread.

That sounds obvious. It is harder to hold than it looks.

This changes the question you ask. The useful question is which parts of a job you can hand off and which you have to keep. Take the all-hands script. AI can give you a structure and a serviceable first draft in a minute, and on a routine quarter that gets you perhaps 70 to 80 percent of the way there. The rest is the part that was always yours: what the message should say, whether the tone fits a room that has just heard about a hiring freeze, which figures are safe to commit to out loud. If you do not run an all-hands, the same split turns up in the update you post to your team channel or the note you send round after a decision.
What "realistic" looks like day to day

Being realistic here means knowing roughly what to expect before you ask. You are then neither surprised when AI delivers nor caught out when it does not, and your attention goes to the parts that need it.

content_blocks.text: Older software could only find, sort, and count what already existed. Generative AI writes something new on demand: a draft, a summary, a plan that did not exist a moment ago.

Artificial intelligence has meant a lot of things over the decades. The part that actually changed how work gets done is one branch, generative AI, and it is worth being precise about what sets it apart. If you lead a team, this is the shift you are now setting the tone for. If you lead no one, it is the same shift landing on your own desk, and the mechanics do not change either way.
What "generative" actually means

Traditional software follows rules a person wrote in advance. A spreadsheet adds the numbers you type in. A search engine returns pages that already exist somewhere. A database hands back the record you asked for. In every case the output was already there in some form, waiting to be retrieved or calculated, and the same input gives the same result every time because someone specified exactly what to do.

Generative AI works from patterns instead of fixed rules. Hand it your scattered notes on how your team runs its release process and it can draft a clean wiki entry that existed nowhere until you asked. Nobody wrote a rule for your particular request. The model produces a response that fits the shape of what you asked for, assembled fresh.
Why this is a different category, not just better software

The distinction has real consequences. It changes both what you can safely hand off and what you have to watch for.

Because the output is generated rather than retrieved, it comes back fluent, fast, and shaped to your request. That is exactly why it helps with drafting that wiki entry, turning a long recorded meeting into a short list of decisions, or putting a dense policy clause into plain language. Work that used to mean sitting down and producing prose from a blank page can now start from a draft.

That same quality is the catch. Retrieved information is either in the system or it is not. Generated content always comes back looking complete and confident, whether or not it is correct. You are no longer running arithmetic you can trust by default. You are reading something that has to be judged on its merits before you rely on it.

Two habits follow from how the technology works. First, generative AI helps most where producing a first version is the slow part: drafting, summarising, restructuring, reformatting. Give it the blank-page job and refine from there.

Second, treat what comes back as a capable draft rather than a finished answer. It is written to look right, which is a different thing from being right. Most of this track is about knowing where that line sits and how to stay on the useful side of it.

content_blocks.text: Every AI tool works inside two hard limits: how it chops your text into pieces, and how much of it the model can hold at once. Knowing where those limits sit is the difference between a reliable answer and one built on material the model has already lost sight of.

The model does not read your input the way you do. Where you see words, paragraphs, and pages, it sees tokens, and it can only hold so many of them at once. Those two facts govern what you can hand a model and what comes back. This lesson covers both.
Tokens: the unit the model reads

A token is a chunk of text, usually a few characters, roughly three-quarters of a word on average. The word "board" is one token. A longer or unusual word might run to two or three. The conversion worth keeping in your head is simple. 1,000 tokens is about 750 words, or a page or two of dense text.

You do not need the maths. You need the instinct. Everything you send and everything the model returns is measured in tokens, and there is a ceiling on how many it can work with at once. A one-line question is a handful of tokens. A spreadsheet export with a few thousand rows, pasted in whole, is tens of thousands. That gap is why the limit turns real on exactly the tasks where AI is most useful, the long and information-dense ones.
The context window: everything the model can see at once

The context window is the total pool of tokens the model can hold in a single conversation. It covers everything in play: the background instructions it starts with, every message you have sent, every reply it has given, and any document or spreadsheet you have pasted or attached. If it is not in the window, the model cannot use it.

This has real consequences for how you work.
What gets cut, and why long chats "forget"

When a conversation or a set of documents outgrows the window, something has to give, and the oldest material falls out of view first. The model does not warn you and does not stop responding. It carries on with less to work from.

This is why a long working session can feel as though the model is forgetting what you told it at the start. It is not a glitch. The detail you set out early has dropped outside the window, and the model is now answering from what remains. The same effect explains why a summary of a very long document can quietly miss what sat on page one, because not all of it was in view when the answer was produced.

A long conversation does not preserve everything you have said. When an early instruction or figure stops being honoured, assume it has fallen out of the window and restate it rather than trusting the model to still hold it.
What this changes about how you hand over work

Modern models have large context windows, hundreds of thousands of tokens, enough to take a full contract, a long email thread, or several files at once. Large is not unlimited. Cleaning up a big spreadsheet export, reformatting a few thousand rows into one consistent structure, is exactly the kind of task that can still reach the edge, and the failure is silent.

The practical moves are straightforward. For a large clean-up, the more you narrow what you hand over to what the task actually needs, the more reliable the result: send the columns that matter, not the whole export, when you can. When you must supply a lot, structure it, because clear headings and labels help the model find what counts inside the pool. And when precision on a specific detail matters, put that detail late and state it plainly rather than assuming an instruction from twenty exchanges ago is still in view.

content_blocks.text: Nobody needs you to type the first draft anymore. They need you to make sure what goes out is right.

If you manage people, you already do a version of this. You brief someone, review what comes back, add context they didn't have, and put your name on the result before it goes anywhere. If you don't manage anyone, the shift is the same, just aimed at your own work instead of someone else's: you're now briefing, reviewing, and signing off on things you used to produce start to finish by yourself.
The bottleneck moved

The old limit on knowledge work was time: hours spent drafting, summarising, formatting, moving information from one shape into another. Much of that can now be handed off. What's left is what was never actually the bottleneck: judgment, context, and the read on what matters and who's in the room. AI didn't change what good work looks like. It just moved the constraint off the mechanical steps and onto you.

This lands harder for people who manage others, because you've spent your career being judged on outcomes you didn't personally produce. The habit of directing rather than doing is already there. What's new is that it now reaches into the drafting and the synthesis too, the parts you might have kept doing yourself out of habit, or because handing them to a person cost more than just doing it. If you've never had anyone to delegate to before, this is that experience for the first time, just aimed at a model instead of a person.
What your contribution becomes

You move from producing to directing. Instead of writing the first draft of a stakeholder update yourself, you write the brief and review what comes back. Instead of reading through a stack of interview notes and building the hiring recommendation single-handed, you direct the first pass and then interrogate it: what did it flatten, what did it miss, what would the hiring committee push back on. Instead of building structure from a blank page, you steer it and sharpen the language.

This sounds like less work. It isn't. Directing well takes more clarity than doing, not less. You have to know what good looks like before you ask for it. You have to catch the error that reads perfectly and is still wrong. And you have to supply the judgment the model can't reach: the history, the politics, the thing that can't go in the recommendation for reasons no prompt would ever surface.
Directing is harder than it sounds. It forces you to know what you want before you ask, and vague direction produces vague work whether it comes from a model or a person.
Three habits that make it work

cards.body: Say what good looks like before you ask for it. One sentence on the goal, the audience, and the shape you want forces enough clarity to get a usable first pass instead of a generic one.
cards.title: Brief before you build

cards.body: Your job is to review and refine, not start over. If you find yourself rewriting everything, the brief was probably the problem, not the output. Fix the instruction and go again instead of grinding through it by hand.
cards.title: Review, do not redo

cards.body: The model does not know your context, your history, or the politics in the room. Every output needs your read on what matters before it leaves your hands. That layer is the part only you can add.
cards.title: Own the judgment layer

content_blocks.text: What this is not

This is not permission to route everything through AI, replace thinking with prompting, or trade accuracy for speed. Push the assembly down and keep the judgment. That is the whole shift. Do it right and the hours you free up go toward the read only you can supply, the part nobody and nothing else can do for you.
The move in one line
Push the assembly down. Keep the judgment. Brief clearly, review honestly, add the context the model cannot see, and own what goes out as your work.

content_blocks.text: When AI hands you something mediocre, the prompt is usually the reason it landed flat, and the prompt is also where you fix it.

Most people who come away unimpressed with AI wrote a vague request and got a vague answer back. The model did its job. It filled the gaps you left, and it filled them with the most generic plausible thing it could reach for. Prompting is a skill, and unlike most skills it improves in minutes, not months. The payoff is immediate, and a sharper instruction turns a throwaway draft into something you can forward, edit lightly, or actually decide from.

This lesson covers the four things that make a prompt good in the first place: specificity, audience, format, and constraints. Whether you are prepping talking points for a vendor negotiation or just trying to get a usable draft of an awkward email, the same four decisions do most of the work. Get them right and most of your frustration disappears.
Specificity: say what you actually want

The most common mistake is asking for too little. "Summarise this document" is a prompt, but it forces the model to guess how long, for whom, and to what end. Now compare that against a fuller version. "Summarise this vendor contract in five bullet points for a non-technical colleague, focusing only on the clauses that carry a cost or a deadline." The second gets you something usable on the first pass. The first gets you a coin flip.

Every guess you leave in a prompt is a decision you have handed to the model, and it will make that decision generically, with no idea what you had in mind. Cutting those guesses is all that specificity means. The extra words are just what it takes to get there.
Vague in, vague out. If the output feels generic, look at your prompt before you blame the model. You almost certainly left the important choices unspecified.
The four levers
For anything you intend to use directly, four decisions carry most of the weight. You will not need all four every time, but naming them takes ten seconds and saves you a round trip.

cards.body: Who is this for? Notes for your own prep read nothing like a message you send to the vendor. State it: for my own use, for a colleague who was not in the room, for a new hire. The model calibrates vocabulary, depth, and what it assumes they already know.
cards.title: Audience

cards.body: What should the output look like? Bullet points, three short paragraphs, a table with named columns, a one-line answer. If you have a shape in mind and do not say so, you get whatever the model defaults to.
cards.title: Format

cards.body: What stance should it take? Neutral analysis, a clear recommendation, or a list of risks only. Asking the model to frame a problem is a different request from asking it to solve one. Decide which you want.
cards.title: Angle

cards.body: What are the hard limits? A word cap, a tone to hold, jargon to avoid. Constraints keep the output inside the box you need it to fit.
cards.title: Constraints

content_blocks.text: Take a real case. You are preparing talking points for a contract renewal with a software vendor who has just proposed a double-digit price increase. "Help me prepare for this negotiation" leaves everything open. Instead: "Draft talking points for our renewal call. We have used this vendor for three years and rely on it daily. They want a large annual increase, and I want to hold it near inflation and add two user seats. Give me three opening positions and the likely pushback on each. Direct, businesslike tone, no filler, one page." Audience, format, angle, and constraints, all decided by you rather than left to the model.
Constraints work in the negative, too

Telling the model what to avoid is as powerful as telling it what to do, and most people never do it. If the output keeps coming back with the same flaw, name the flaw.

The patterns that come up most: "Do not open with a preamble. Start with the first point." "Do not suggest fixes; I only want the problem framed." "Do not use corporate filler like leverage, synergy, or holistic." "Do not exceed 200 words." None of these is a nitpick. A recurring annoyance you keep editing out by hand is a one-line instruction you have not written yet.
If you find yourself deleting the same thing from every output, stop deleting and start excluding. Name it in the prompt.
Anatomy of a strong prompt

The difference is intention, not creativity. Watch what happens when the four levers meet a weak request.

**Weak:** "Write talking points for my vendor call."

**Strong:** "Write talking points for a 30-minute renewal call with our IT vendor. Open with the value we have had from them, then make the case that their proposed increase runs above market, and close with the two concessions I need to walk away satisfied. Firm but friendly tone, under 250 words, no header."

The strong version came from decisions made up front rather than a better imagination. It said who it is for, what shape it takes, what it should do, and what it must not do. That is all it comes down to.
A note on where this goes next

You can push quality further with heavier techniques, such as showing the model a worked example of what good looks like, or giving it a role to shift its perspective, like asking it to pressure-test your talking points the way the vendor account manager would. Those are genuine multipliers, and they get their own lesson. For now, the four levers plus a clear statement of what to avoid will handle most of your work. Master the baseline before reaching for the extras.
The habit worth building

Before you send a prompt for anything that matters, run a two-second check: have I said who it is for, what it should look like, what stance to take, and what to avoid? You will skip some of those on purpose, and that is fine. The point is that you decided, instead of leaving the model to guess. That habit separates the people who find AI useful from the people who find it disappointing.

questions.explanation: The third names the format (five talking points), the context and goal (hold the increase near inflation), and the tone. Those decisions are what turn a coin-flip response into something usable. Professional is too vague to act on.
options: Help me prepare for the vendor renewal call.
Give me some good talking points for the vendor call, and make them professional.
Draft five talking points for a renewal call with our analytics vendor, aimed at holding their proposed increase near inflation, in a firm but friendly tone.
Can you help me think through this vendor negotiation?

options: Regenerate until one comes back without the preamble.

Switch to a more capable model.

questions.explanation: Strength comes from intention, not word count or creativity. Every choice you do not make, the model makes for you, usually generically. Roles and worked examples help, but they are not what makes a baseline prompt good.
options: The strong one is longer and uses more advanced vocabulary.
The strong one makes the decisions, audience, format, angle, and constraints, instead of leaving them to the model.
The strong one asks the model to be creative.

title: How to write a good prompt

content_blocks.text: Take the folder of raw meeting notes sitting in your week, the ones that still need turning into decisions, owners, and next steps. This lesson runs that one task from start to finish.

Everything so far has built toward a single ability: taking work you actually own, putting an AI tool to it, and keeping enough judgement in the loop to trust what comes out. Here you do it on something real. The task you pick should be one you would have had to do this week anyway, not a demo.
Choose the right task to start with

The best first task is one you do often, that eats real time, and where you can tell good output from bad because you know the subject. That last point matters most. If you cannot judge the result, you cannot catch what AI gets wrong, and this lesson is as much about building your eye as about saving time.

Skip anything that touches a hard no-go zone. Final decisions that carry legal or personal weight, confidential material that cannot go into your tool, work where a plausible-but-wrong answer would slip through unnoticed. You already hold those judgements. Apply them before you start, not after.

One task fits almost any role and makes a good first run: turning a pile of messy meeting notes into a clean list of decisions, owners, and open questions. Whatever you choose, it should be real work with a deadline you already have.
Run it through, step by step
Set up the prompt

Start with the four things every prompt needs: the task, the audience, the format you want, and any constraints. If you have a strong example of what good looks like, paste it in; a model matches a shown standard far better than a described one. Give it the source material it needs and nothing it should not have.

For your meeting notes, hand over the raw text and tell the model to keep firm decisions separate from open questions rather than blur the two, and to attach an owner to every action it can find one for.
Read the first output like an editor, not a reader

The first pass is a draft. Read it the way you would scrutinise a colleague's proposal before it goes up, hunting for gaps, weak claims, and lines that sound right but are not. Check anything factual against the source. A figure, a name, or a date the model produced on its own is exactly where a hallucination hides. If the task list names a deadline or an owner that appears nowhere in the notes, that is your signal to check before you send it on.
Refine, do not restart

Most first drafts land close but wrong in a specific way. Too long, the wrong emphasis, a section that missed the point. Name the fix and ask again, and keep the thread going while it is still improving. Start fresh only when the output has drifted so far that correcting it costs more than a clean prompt would. Knowing which situation you are in is the instinct you have been building all along.

cards.body: Each turn gets closer. Your corrections land, and the model holds the context and builds on it. When that is happening, keep steering from inside the same conversation.
cards.title: Stay in the thread

cards.body: Corrections stop sticking, the output contradicts an earlier turn, or you are spending more effort patching than a clean prompt would take. When that is the pattern, reset with a sharper opening prompt.
cards.title: Start fresh

content_blocks.text: Close the loop: you own what leaves your hands

When the output is good enough, it is still yours. Do the final read as the person accountable for it, because you are. Confirm the facts hold, the tone fits the audience, and nothing confidential slipped in along the way. Then send it, file it, or carry it into the meeting as your own work.
This goes out under your name. Verification is the step that makes the speed safe to rely on, and skipping it means standing behind a draft you never actually checked.

Do this once with a real task and something shifts. The abstract advice from earlier modules turns into a workflow you can feel. You see where AI saved you an hour, where your judgement was the thing that mattered, and where you would push harder next time. That felt sense is worth more than any single output. It is what lets you take on the next task with confidence and know exactly what to check.
What you should notice by the end

You moved from doing the task to directing it. You set the frame, supplied the context, judged the drafts, corrected what was off, and verified before anything left your hands. That is the whole track in one pass, and it repeats on the next task, and the one after that.

options: Keep refining until it converges
Lower your standard and accept it
Start fresh with a sharper opening prompt

title: Work through a real recurring task with AI

content_blocks.text: A model fails in a handful of predictable places. The same weak points turn up again and again, whatever you happen to be working on. Learn where they sit and you can keep working fast and still catch the bad output before it reaches anyone.

Picture the budget you are pulling together ahead of a decision meeting: last quarter's actuals, a couple of forecasts, and a recommendation on where the money should go next. A model can draft most of that in minutes. It can also get four specific things wrong, in ways that survive a quick read and land in the room looking finished. This lesson walks through those four, where the mechanism you have already met, plausible text rather than looked-up fact, does its most reliable damage, and what each one costs you.
Stale information

A model knows what it was trained on, up to a cutoff date, and nothing after it. Ask it about a tax threshold that changed last quarter, a supplier that raised its rates in March, or a regulation amended since its training, and it answers with the same steady confidence it uses for facts that have held for a decade. It has no built-in sense that its knowledge expires.

The cost hides in plain sight, because the answer reads as current. A budget built on last year's rates. A pricing recommendation resting on market conditions that have since moved. A cost line that misses a supplier increase half the room already knows about. Each one reads perfectly, and each is quietly out of date. Unless the tool is pulling live data, treat anything time-sensitive as a draft you still have to date-check.
Weak arithmetic and quantitative reasoning

On its own, a model writes the text of a calculation. It does not run the calculation. It generates the digits that most plausibly follow the words "the total is", which is a different act from adding the numbers up. Some tools now run real code and compute exactly, and where that happens the maths is genuine. Until you know a real calculation ran, treat every figure as text shaped like a number.

It often lands close, and close is the dangerous part: a total that is off by a little slips past the review a wildly absurd number never would. This bites hardest in the very work you would most want to hand off. Summing the columns in a budget, working out a percentage change on a forecast, or reconciling two totals that should agree are the moments the model looks most useful and is least reliable. Multi-step reasoning breaks the same way. Each step reads as sound, the chain compounds one small slip, and the conclusion arrives confident and wrong.

The more a task turns on numbers or a chain of logical steps, the less its answer is worth at face value. And the more it looks like the model just saved you the effort, the more of that effort has simply moved to checking it.
Bias

A model learned from an enormous body of human writing, and it absorbed the patterns there, including the skewed ones. Ask it to sketch a candidate for a senior role, name a typical customer, or describe who does what on a team, and its defaults track the majority patterns in its training data rather than the people actually in front of you.

This surfaces in two places. In anything that touches people, such as hiring language, performance notes, or assumptions about an audience, the model can dress a stereotype up as professional-sounding prose. And when you ask it to weigh options, it leans toward the conventional, mainstream take, which makes it a poor source of real contrarian challenge. Left unchecked, it narrows your thinking at the exact moment you wanted it widened. If you manage no one, the same caution holds for your own work. The vendor shortlist it drafts or the survey comments it summarises inherit its defaults, not your read of the situation.
Reasoning gaps

The model is fluent, and fluency reads as competence. It does not reliably hold a complex argument together. It will miss the load-bearing assumption in a proposal, accept a flawed premise you hand it, or contradict something it claimed three paragraphs earlier, none of it flagged.

The sharper risk is agreeableness. Push back on its answer and it will often fold and reverse, whether or not you had a point. Frame a question so it implies the answer you are hoping for and it tends to hand that answer straight back. So when you ask it to stress-test the case for a budget before the meeting, it makes a weak challenger: better at producing a first pass than at judging whether that pass holds up. Honest friction is the one thing you most want there, and the one thing it is least able to give.
What this costs, in one line

None of these failures announces itself. Whether the output is right or wrong, it comes back equally fluent, formatted, and confident. The error you spot is cheap; you fix it and move on. The expensive one is the plausible mistake that reads perfectly and gets forwarded: a stale rate in the budget, a total that does not add up in the pricing case, a stereotype in a job description, an assumption nobody challenged sitting under a recommendation. That is how AI usually fails at work. It hands you a confident, well-dressed mistake, and the mistake goes out under your name.

content_blocks.text: Where AI earns its keep

AI is strongest when the work is open-ended language and weakest when it turns on facts, figures, or judgment only you can supply. A project post-mortem sits right on that line. The write-up, the timeline, the tidy list of what happened: that is language work, and AI is fast at it. What actually went wrong, and what your team should do differently: that stays with you. Whether you are chairing the review or just accounting for your own part of the project, the split lands the same way.

Think in task categories, not tools. The same model that turns your scattered incident notes into a clean timeline in seconds will also name the wrong root cause with total confidence. What changed between those two results is the kind of task you handed it, not the tool.
The four things it does well
Most of what AI genuinely accelerates falls into four buckets. They share a trait: the value is in producing fluent language or structure, and a human still owns the final call.

cards.body: Open-ended work with words: writing, summarising, reasoning through a problem out loud. Hand it your scattered post-mortem notes and it returns a first-pass timeline with decisions, owners, and open questions. What comes back is a rough document you then shape further.
cards.title: Thinking and drafting

cards.body: Turning information from one form into another: a requirements list into a table, a dense policy clause into plain language, raw notes into a slide outline. Reliable, because the source material sits right in front of it.
cards.title: Structured transformation

cards.body: Emails, summaries, the opening draft of the post-mortem writeup itself. You get something usable in seconds and spend your time refining instead of staring at a blank page.
cards.title: First-draft generation

cards.body: Pulling together what is generally known about a topic into a starting map: a quick primer on how other teams run blameless retros, say, that you then check and sharpen against your own situation.
cards.title: Broad synthesis

content_blocks.text: The pattern across all four: AI is fast at the first 80 percent of language work. The last 20 percent stays with you: the accuracy, the judgment, the sign-off.
The four places it falls short

The limits are just as predictable. They cluster where the task stops being about producing plausible language and starts being about something the model cannot reliably do.

**Calculation and live facts.** On its own, a language model does not calculate. It produces text that looks like a computed answer, and it has no live data unless a tool feeds it some. So when a post-mortem draft says the outage lasted 47 minutes or that response times tripled, treat those as text shaped like numbers until you check them against the actual logs. Both limits lift when the tool is wired for it, since some now run real code or reach a live source. Unless you know that is happening, a duration or a cost it hands you is a claim to verify rather than a figure it worked out.

**Novel judgment with no clear right answer.** Deciding what really caused the slip, and what to change next time, is the part of the post-mortem that matters most. When that call turns on competing accounts of what happened, or on which risk is worth carrying, AI gives you something generic and reasonable-sounding. It cannot make the trade-off for you, because the trade-off depends on what you know and value, not on what plausibly comes next. That holds whether you run the review or simply speak to your own slice of it.

**Anything needing context it does not have.** The model has what you told it and what it absorbed in training. The real reason a project stalled is often the thing nobody wrote down: the deadline that was political, the corner someone was quietly told to cut, the disagreement that never made the minutes. None of that reached the model. Missing context does not stop it from answering. It answers as if the gap were not there.

**High-stakes precision work.** Financial modelling, regulatory decisions, anything carrying legal or safety weight. The task itself demands an exactness the model does not guarantee, so it sits outside what you can hand over and accept as-is.
Across every category, one rule holds: AI output is a starting point a human checks, never a finished product you forward untouched.
Ask whether it needs AI at all

Part of the skill is knowing when not to reach for it. A recurring email wants a saved template. A known process wants a checklist. A single fact wants an ordinary search. Pointing a language model at work that a plain search or a saved template would handle faster and more reliably is its own small mistake. What you are after is the outcome, and often the older tool gets you there sooner.
The instinct to build

Before you hand off a piece of the post-mortem, run one quick test: is this mostly about producing language and structure, or does it turn on a number, a fact, or a judgment about what really happened? The first kind AI does well and fast. The second it will answer anyway, confidently and often wrong. Learning to feel that difference before you delegate is most of what separates the people who get real value from AI from the people who do not.

title: What AI is good at, and where it falls short

content_blocks.text: A colleague hands you a paragraph of dense technical language, a clause on data residency, say, and asks you to make it readable for the whole company. Stripping the jargon is a clean hand-off to a model. Deciding which caveat cannot be simplified away without making the result quietly wrong is not.

You already run this calculation whenever you pass a task to someone else, weighing what it costs to brief and check them against what it costs to just do it yourself. Handing work to AI is the same discipline with one difference. The model is fast and never tires, but it arrives with none of your context, and it carries none of the accountability when the call turns out wrong. If you manage nobody and have never delegated a thing, the same judgment still applies, aimed at your own work: which parts to hand off, and which to keep because only you can do them right.
The two questions that decide it

Before you hand anything off, ask two things.

First, how much task-specific context does this need? Context the model cannot pull from the words in front of it: who is in the room, why a timeline really slipped, which stakeholder is privately opposed. For the plain-language rewrite, the context that matters is narrow. Which regulatory detail is load-bearing and which is decoration, and you can hand that over in a sentence. When a task turns on context you cannot supply that cheaply, either keep it or brief the model properly first. When it needs little, it is a strong candidate to pass on.

Second, what does a subtle error cost, and how easily would you catch one? A mistake that jumps out on a quick read is cheap, because you see it, you fix it, you move on. A mistake only an insider would notice is expensive, because it can pass review and reach a decision-maker intact. In the translation case, a dropped qualifier that changes what the clause actually permits is that kind of quiet, costly error. The harder a mistake is to catch, the more the task belongs with you.

The dangerous combination is high context plus errors that are hard to catch: fluent, confident output that looks right and is wrong in a way only you would spot. That is where the time AI saved comes back to cost you, with interest.
Where the time saving is real

AI pays off on structured, repetitive work, and on moving information from one shape into another. Summarising a long thread. Turning rough notes into a clean table. Rewriting that dense clause in plain words. The quality bar is clear enough for the model to hit, the time saved is genuine, and mistakes tend to surface on review.

Underneath most good delegation sits a split you can make on almost any task: separate the judgment from the assembly. Deciding which findings belong in a report is judgment, so keep it. Writing those findings up once you have chosen them is assembly, so pass it on. Deciding which technical nuance must survive a translation is judgment. Producing the clean plain-language draft around that decision is assembly.

That split is why so much real work is neither fully kept nor fully handed off. You do the thinking; the model does the production.
What to keep

Keep the work whose value lives in the parts a model cannot supply. Novel judgment calls with no obvious right answer and competing risks. Anything that depends on having been in the room. Anything where the output has to reflect your read of the politics, the history, or the people involved.

The model will always give you an answer, and that is the risk. Ask it to recommend a pricing change and it will recommend one, fluently, drawing on nothing about your market, your margins, or your competitors. The answer comes out generic, and your value on that task was the non-generic part. When a task turns on knowing something the model cannot know, holding onto it is exactly where you add value.
A working map

cards.body: Summarising an interview or a long thread. Rewriting a dense clause in plain language. Drafting a standard status update. Writing up findings you have already chosen. Clear quality bar, visible errors, real time saved.
cards.title: Delegate

cards.body: Deciding what goes in the report. Recommending an approach. Choosing which nuance a translation cannot lose. Any call that turns on context the model cannot have: the room, the history, the politics. Generic is not good enough here.
cards.title: Keep

cards.body: Most real work. You supply the judgment, then hand over the assembly. Decide the risks, then let the model draft the write-up. Spot-check and prioritise what comes back.
cards.title: Split

content_blocks.text: A caution before you rely on this map. Handing the model a task that needs context you never gave it does not make the task easier; it makes the output confidently generic. And splitting well depends on doing the judgment part yourself first. Delegate the decision along with the drafting, and the effort you thought you saved is gone. You have handed away the part that was yours to own.

questions.explanation: The judgment, choosing the caveat that has to survive, is already done and is yours to own. Rewriting the clause in plain words around that decision is assembly, which is what the model is good at. Hand over the drafting, keep the decision.

Ask it to draft the plain-language version around the caveat you have already flagged, then check it
Keep the whole task, since anything with legal nuance should stay with you
Ask it to suggest an entirely different set of caveats as a cross-check

questions.explanation: Context is the first filter. If the task turns on things the model cannot know, either keep it or supply that context first. Time saved and complexity matter, but they come after this question.
options: How long the task would take you to do by hand
How much task-specific context it needs that the model cannot get from your words
Whether the task is technically complex
Whether other people on your team already use AI for it
questions.q: What is the primary filter for deciding whether to hand a task to AI?

questions.explanation: The model will always produce an answer. On a judgment call, that answer is generic because it lacks your specific context, and the value of the task lived in the non-generic part. That is what makes it a keep.
options: Models are not allowed to give recommendations
It will refuse without a system prompt
It will produce a fluent answer, but a generic one that ignores your market, history, and constraints
A recommendation takes longer to review than to write
